newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Opposition leader attacks govt budget plans.
newsitem.headline: Opposition leader attacks govt budget plans.

text.p: Portugal's main opposition party slammed the minority Socialist government's 1997 budget on Wednesday, as parliament was due to begin debating the plan, saying it took the easy route to meeting single currency goals.

Social Democrat leader Marcelo Rebelo de Sousa accused the Socialists of ducking tough issues such as reform to the social security and health systems and relying heavily on boosting tax income to meet next year's deficit target.

But in an interview with the Diario Economico, Rebelo de Sousa stopped short of saying his party, the largest in parliament after the Socialists, would vote against the budget package which is crucial to Portugal's hopes of winning a place in Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) in 1999.
"First, we are going to hear what the government has to say," the opposition leader said.
Parliament, in which the Socialists are four seats short of an outright majority, starts debating the general aims of the 1997 budget on Wednesday with a vote set for Friday.
But the legislature will only get down to detailed study of the programme in December with a final vote scheduled for December 11.
The Socialists have 112 seats in the 230-seat parliament against 88 for the Social Democrats. The remainder are split between the anti-European Popular Party and the Communists.

Prime Minister Antonio Guterres has warned that he will not accept any changes to the budget plan that jeopardise the target of a deficit below the three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) ceiling set for entry to EMU.
He has hinted that he would seek fresh elections if defeated in the legislature where the Popular Party and the Communists are likely to reject the budget proposals.

Rebelo de Sousa, who told Reuters in early October that he would let the Socialists drive the budget through parliament if the alternative were an early ballot, reaffirmed his view that elections next year would be an act of "political irresponsibility."

Rebelo de Sousa said that the Socialists, who won power in elections in October 1995 after a decade of Social Democrat rule, should have taken the opportunity to begin reforming the expensive social security and health systems.
"The point open to most criticism in this budget is the fact that it is seeking to cut the deficit with one-off rather than structural measures," he told Diario Economico.
